title: Dîner après le théâtre  (Dinner After the Theatre)

segments.t: Following his brilliant theatrical performance, acclaimed actor Fabrice Luchini meets Andréa Martel for a late dinner. The pair exchange warm compliments and playful relationship advice in high spirits before their evening is interrupted. Listen to the scene in French first. Don't worry about catching every word.
Bonsoir Andréa! Tu es très élégante.
Merci Fabrice. Bravo pour ton spectacle!
C'était vraiment une pièce magnifique.
Tu as aimé ma prestation?
J'ai absolument adoré ton jeu.
Et cette jeune femme blonde d'hier?
Non, ce n'est pas mon genre.
Elle te plaît beaucoup. Fonce!
Tu crois vraiment que ça marcherait?
C'est tout à fait évident!
Je ne sais pas par où commencer.
Fais-moi confiance pour l'amour.
On mange quelque chose maintenant?
Oui, commandons un bon dîner.
Now let's break down the scene step by step. Listen to each line, followed by its meaning and a short explanation.
Bonsoir Andréa! Tu es très élégante.
'Good evening Andréa! You look very elegant.' Fabrice opens with a standard evening greeting, joined by a clear cognate. You will hear this in French.
Merci Fabrice. Bravo pour ton spectacle!
'Thank you Fabrice. Bravo on your show!' Andréa congratulates him using a handy chunk meaning 'bravo on', followed by his performance. This is perfectly natural in French.
C'était vraiment une pièce magnifique.
'It was truly a magnificent play.' You'll hear a past description meaning 'it was', paired with a cognate meaning 'magnificent'. In French, it works nicely.
Tu as aimé ma prestation?
'Did you like my performance?' He asks a question using the casual 'you' and a past action meaning 'liked'. The French use this a lot.
J'ai absolument adoré ton jeu.
'I absolutely loved your acting.' She answers with a strong past action meaning 'adored', preceded by a cognate. In French, it sounds perfect.
Et cette jeune femme blonde d'hier?
'And that young blonde woman from yesterday?' Fabrice turns to gossip, using a handy chunk meaning 'yesterday'. This is standard in French.
Non, ce n'est pas mon genre.
'No, she is not my type.' Andréa brushes him off with a handy sentence literally meaning 'it is not my genre'. A nice sentence in French.
Elle te plaît beaucoup. Fonce!
'You like her very much. Go for it!' The second part is a colloquial spoken command meaning 'charge' or 'rush in'. A great expression in French.
Tu crois vraiment que ça marcherait?
'Do you really think that would work?' The opening uses the casual 'you' and an action meaning 'believe' or 'think'. You can say this in French.
C'est tout à fait évident!
'It is completely obvious!' Fabrice insists with a handy chunk meaning 'completely', finishing with a cognate. In French, this is widely used.
Je ne sais pas par où commencer.
'I do not know where to start.' In the negative, the action 'know' is wrapped by two pieces, followed by 'where'. The French love this expression.
Fais-moi confiance pour l'amour.
'Trust me when it comes to love.' He poses as an expert using a handy expression meaning 'make me trust'. In French, it fits perfectly.
On mange quelque chose maintenant?
'Shall we eat something now?' He suggests food using the everyday spoken 'we', joined by a handy chunk meaning 'something'. A nice way to say it in French.
Oui, commandons un bon dîner.

'Yes, let us order a good dinner.' She agrees with an enthusiastic 'yes', followed by a group command to order. In French, it is a great choice. Now let's listen to the entire exchange once more from beginning to end.

Merci Fabrice. Bravo pour ton spectacle!

Fabrice Luchini and Andréa bond over theatrical art and romantic advice over dinner. Remember the colloquial French encouragement for seizing an opportunity: fonce. See you next time!
À demain!
